abstract: Accurate gravity-field reconstruction around irregular small bodies is critical for safe close-proximity operations in deep-space missions. Classical mascon models are physically interpretable but are tied to static grids, limiting their ability to represent localized high-frequency anomalies without heavy discretization. Implicit neural gravity representations can be accurate, yet are often expensive for dense evaluation and may exhibit near-surface artifacts. We propose Differentiable Mascons (DM), a physicsconstrained spatial–mass joint optimization framework for explicit asteroid gravity inversion. DM liberates mascons from rigid grids and jointly optimizes their masses and 3D coordinates using differentiable gravity residuals. Physical validity is ensured by construction via a smooth non-negative mass parameterization and a shape-informed optimizer-state pruning strategy that keeps mascons inside the target body. A gradient-driven adaptive resampling mechanism further reallocates mascons toward high-error regions to better capture localized anomalies. Experiments on a highly heterogeneous asteroid benchmark across multiple orbital altitudes show that DM consistently outperforms static-grid mascons and implicitnetwork baselines, reducing far-field relative errors by up to an order of magnitude. Visualizations also indicate improved recovery of salient internal heterogeneity in our synthetic experiments.

blocks.html: Recent asteroid exploration missions—including NEAR Shoemaker at Eros [1], Hayabusa and Hayabusa2 at Itokawa and Ryugu [2], and OSIRIS-REx at Bennu [3]— demand highly accurate gravity field models for safe proximity operations, low-altitude orbit determination, and surface sampling. This task is inherently challenging because small bodies often present highly irregular shapes and heterogeneous interiors, inducing strong spatial variability in the near-field gravity. In this work, we focus on reconstructing the external gravitational acceleration field and an equivalent internal mass distribution around an irregular body from sampled gravity observations.

Common parameterizations for gravity reconstruction include spherical harmonics [4], polyhedral gravity models [5], and mass concentrations (mascons) [6]. While spherical harmonics can be ill-conditioned for highly irregular bodies and polyhedral models often assume uniform density in their basic form, mascon models offer a simple, physically interpretable alternative. By approximating the body via discrete point-mass superposition, mascons naturally accommodate physical constraints (e.g., non-negativity, shape bounds) and are highly efficient for orbital dynamics evaluations. However, traditional mascons are typically bound to static grid topologies, requiring excessive discretization to represent short-wavelength, localized anomalies.

Alongside these classical techniques, recent years have seen growing interest in machine learning for space geodesy [7, 8]. In this context, implicit neural representations (e.g., GeodesyNet [9]) have been introduced to model continuous density fields for gravity inversion. Though highly expressive, implicit networks can suffer from localized error concentrations near the surface and computational overhead during dense query evaluations around the target body. Conversely, explicit structured mascon variants (e.g., MasconCube [10]) significantly improve computational efficiency but still lack geometric adaptivity: capturing sharp internal contrasts requires substantially increasing the static grid resolution.

To bridge this gap, we propose Differentiable Mascons (DM), a physics-constrained spatial–mass joint optimization framework that retains the efficiency and physical transparency of explicit mascons while substantially improving adaptivity. By liberating mascons from rigid grids, DM jointly optimizes their 3D coordinates and masses via gradient-driven residual feedback, adaptively reallocating representational capacity toward anomalous regions at a fixed number of mascon parameters (N).
Core contributions are:

• Continuous spatial–mass joint optimization. A differentiable formulation enabling discrete mascons to dynamically adjust their locations and masses, adaptively responding to local gravity residuals.
• Physics-constrained parameterization. Physical validity is enforced by construction via a smooth non-negative mass mapping and a shape-informed
optimizer-state pruning strategy that strictly confines mascons within the physical boundaries.

• Adaptive recovery of internal heterogeneity.A gradient-driven resampling mechanism that actively captures sharp density interfaces. In our synthetic benchmark, DM successfully reconstructs internal heterogeneous mass distributions consistent with the ground truth, demonstrating its capability to infer complex internal structures solely from external gravity observations.

We propose Differentiable Mascons (DM), a continuous and differentiable framework for spatial–mass joint inversion of an asteroid gravity field under a fixed mascon budget. DM jointly optimizes mascon masses and 3D locations with first-order gradients, enforces physical feasibility through a smooth nonnegativity mapping and a shape-informed interior repair, and reallocates model capacity using a residual-driven adaptive resampling mechanism.

This section establishes a continuous and differentiable framework for spatial–mass joint inversion in an asteroid mascon model. The key idea is to optimize mascon masses and locations jointly with an adaptive momentum optimizer, while enforcing physical feasibility through a smooth constrained parameterization and a shape-informed feasibility treatment for mascon positions. In addition, we introduce a residual-driven spatial reconfiguration mechanism so that the mascon array can directly respond to local gravity mismatches by reallocating representational capacity toward poorly explained regions.

To evaluate whether the proposed Differentiable Mascons (DM) framework effectively captures interior structures and reproduces external gravity fields, we perform a rigorous closed-loop validation. We benchmark DM against the implicit GeodesyNet [9] and the explicit MasconCube [10] using the highly heterogeneous Eros-Three-Regions synthetic dataset [10].

For numerical stability, the asteroid geometry is normalized into a bounding box of [−0.8, 0.8]3. During training, we uniformly sample 20,000 query points in the exterior space within a normalized distance of r ≤1.0, strictly filtering out all interior points via a ray–triangle intersection test against the surface mesh to maintain physical validity. The reference (observed) accelerations are generated directly from the ground-truth mascon model used to construct the dataset. To decouple dimensionless mass scaling from topological evaluation, we compute the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Mean Relative Error (MRE) using a scale-invariant least-squares projection [9].

Gravity-field prediction accuracy depends strongly on observation distance: near-surface measurements are more sensitive to localized, high-frequency variations, while higher-altitude evaluations emphasize global consistency as the field becomes smoother with distance. To rigorously test both regimes, we follow standard multi-altitude evaluation protocols [9] by randomly sampling 10,000 unseen evaluation points at each of three fixed normalized altitudes (0.05, 0.10, and 0.25). All methods are evaluated on these exact same validation sets to ensure a strictly fair comparison.

Table 1 reports the mean absolute error (MAE) and mean relative error (MRE) at each altitude for GeodesyNet, MasconCube, and the proposed DM. DM achieves the lowest errors at all three altitudes under both criteria, indicating consistently improved accuracy from the challenging nearfield regime to the smoother far-field regime. Notably, in the near-surface setting (Altitude_0.05), DM reduces the MRE to 0.2313% (vs. 0.2458% for MasconCube and 0.4509% for GeodesyNet). This advantage persists and becomes more pronounced at larger distances, reaching an exceptional 0.0169% at Altitude_0.25 (vs. 0.0556% and 0.1340%, respectively). Spatial Distribution of Near-Surface Errors under Heterogeneous Density To emphasize the impact of internal density heterogeneity on near-field gravity prediction, we visualize the 3D spatial distribution of pointwise relative acceleration errors (pointwise MRE) at the most challenging near-surface regime, Altitude_0.05 (Fig. 1). This regime is particularly sensitive to localized mass anomalies: compared with higher-altitude evaluations, near-surface accelerations contain stronger high-frequency signatures induced by density contrasts and sharp internal transitions, which often manifest as spatially clustered residuals on the asteroid’s exterior.

As shown in Fig. 1, GeodesyNet exhibits distinct patches of elevated error (warmer colors) concentrated in specific surface neighborhoods. This behavior is consistent with the ill-posedness of gravity inversion under heterogeneity: different internal density configurations can generate similar external gravitational fields, and the ambiguity becomes more pronounced for geometries/heterogeneity patterns approaching symmetry, where shell-theorem-like cancellations reduce the observability of internal anomalies. In such cases, a purely implicit representation may fit the field in an averaged sense while still leaving systematic, spatially correlated near-field residuals.

MasconCube reduces the overall error level and suppresses part of these high-error pockets, yet localized artifacts remain close to the surface. This is aligned with a known limitation of point-mass (mascon) approximations: discrepancies are most evident near the body, where discretization and geometry–parameterization mismatch can introduce surface-adjacent error structures even when the global field is captured reasonably well.

In contrast, DM presents the most uniform low-error distribution across the entire body in Fig. 1, with markedly fewer and weaker error clusters. This indicates stronger robustness to heterogeneous density distributions. By allowing discrete mass elements to dynamically adjust their spatial coordinates during learning, DLM can better align its effective mass distribution with latent high-density regions and density transitions, thereby mitigating heterogeneityinduced local residuals that otherwise emerge near the surface. Overall, the visualization supports that DLM’s near-field improvement is not only a reduction in average error but also a substantial attenuation of spatially localized errors attributable to internal density non-uniformity and surface-adjacent discretization effects.

blocks.title: Adaptive Reconstruction of Internal Heterogeneous Density

blocks.html: Gravity field inversion is inherently an ill-posed physical problem: infinitely many internal mass distributions can produce the exact same external gravity field. To verify whether the DLM framework genuinely learned the true internal physical structure of the asteroid rather than merely overfitting the external gravitational field, we conducted a cross-sectional visualization analysis of the internal mass distribution.

blocks.html: By employing Gaussian kernel density estimation based on Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) principles, we transformed the discrete mascon parameters into continuous macroscopic density fields, as shown in Figure 2. The visualization yields highly encouraging results that highlight the fundamental advantage of spatial adaptivity.

As observed in Row (a), the rigid orthogonal grid parameterization of MasconCube forces the internal mass to homogenize. It completely fails to capture the underlying structural complexities, resulting in a blurred internal profile tainted by visible grid artifacts.

In stark contrast, even without any prior knowledge of the internal topology, our DLM framework (Row b) faithfully reconstructs the concealed "Three-Regions" heterogeneous structure, closely mirroring the absolute Ground Truth (Row c). The physical impact of our two core operators is explicitly observable from these SPH-smoothed cross-sections: First, owing to the shape-informed optimizer state pruning, there is absolutely no fictitious mass wandering outside the physical boundaries; the density strictly drops to zero at the asteroid’s surface. Second, driven by the adaptive resampling and joint spatial–mass optimization, the mascons autonomously break the static grid limitations. They spontaneously cluster to form distinct internal density interfaces, capturing the intricate structural voids (deep purple) and localized dense aggregates (bright yellow) with remarkable fidelity.

This qualitative comparison substantiates that our framework possesses the robust capability to autonomously decouple complex internal physical heterogeneities solely from external gravitational observations, effectively regularizing the ill-posed inversion problem.

blocks.html: We introduced Differentiable Mascons (DM), a physicsconstrained spatial–mass joint inversion framework for small-body geodesy. By coupling coordinate optimization with gradient-driven resampling, DM overcomes the discretization artifacts of static grids and the near-surface error concentrations of implicit networks. Evaluations on a highly heterogeneous benchmark demonstrate that DM reduces far-field relative errors by up to an order of magnitude and successfully recovers concealed internal density patterns solely from external gravity fields. Future work will integrate real spacecraft radiometric tracking measurements and jointly estimate dynamical rotational states.
